decisions.reason: The question asks whether highlighting helps readers spot code that needs review. It omits how highlighting affects editing and whether highlighting likely edits works better than highlighting low-probability tokens.
The method says the edit model highlights tokens likely to be edited. It omits the preliminary data from nine coders who corrected Codex outputs until the tasks were completed properly.

The poster gives 30 participants and three easy LeetCode tasks. It omits the participants’ Python experience and employment at a large US technology company, as well as randomization of task order and tool-to-task assignments.
The method correctly identifies the shared Codex model, the three presentation conditions, and both thresholds. It omits that the thresholds equalized total highlight counts across the three tasks.

The three means and both p-values are correct, and the caption gives the 10-minute cap. The result leaves readers to infer that p = 0.003 indicates a significant advantage and p = 0.06 indicates only a trend.

Panel (b) shows the expected pattern and approximate survival rates. The caption leaves token survival undefined, and the poster gives neither the exact rates nor an explanation of how the pattern shows more localized editing.
Panel (c) shows higher preference for Edit model highlights. The poster omits the exact ratings, p-value, survey topics, and reverse coding of the distraction item.
The poster omits that the edit model was trained on the same completions evaluated in the study and that comparable effects on unseen tasks remain unverified.
The poster omits that effects on oversight accuracy and automation bias remain untested.
